name: Cassini (Cassini–Huygens mission)

destinations.note: Orbited Saturn for 13 years, then deliberately plunged into its atmosphere and burned up in 2017.

dateNotes: Saturn orbit insertion: July 1, 2004 UTC (June 30 in California time).
The Huygens probe, built by the European Space Agency, landed on Titan on January 14, 2005; Titan is not a separate destination on this site.

status.text: Deliberately burned up in Saturn's atmosphere on September 15, 2017 — no longer exists

finalFate: With little propellant left for course corrections, the team ended the mission with 22 dives between Saturn and its rings (the 'Grand Finale'), then a final plunge into the atmosphere, sending data until it burned up. The goal: protect moons that might support life, such as Enceladus and Titan, from contamination.

location.description: No spacecraft remains: Cassini burned up in Saturn's atmosphere.

primary.title: A camera that caught ice fountains
primary.howItWorks: Cassini flew close to the little moon Enceladus many times, taking pictures and measuring what was around it.
primary.knowledge: Scientists saw fountains of water vapor and ice shooting from its south pole, and understood there is water under its ice.

secondary.title: From a 'hint' to an 'ocean world': the chain of evidence at Enceladus
secondary.howItWorks: During the first close flyby (February 17, 2005) an unexpected hint appeared. Later flybys confirmed a plume shooting water vapor and ice grains at about 400 m/s, and the spacecraft flew through it to analyze its material.
secondary.knowledge: The plume is a direct observation; the global ocean beneath the crust and the signs of hydrothermal activity are conclusions that combine several measurements.

engineeringChallenge.challenge: As propellant ran low, the team had to make sure the spacecraft would never one day crash into a moon that might support life.
engineeringChallenge.solution: Design the 'Grand Finale' orbits — 22 dives between Saturn and its rings to collect new science — then end the mission by entering the atmosphere.

discoveries.text: ESA's Huygens probe landed on Titan on January 14, 2005 — the first landing in the outer Solar System.
Plumes of water vapor and ice shoot from Enceladus's south pole; some material falls back and some feeds Saturn's E ring.
Enceladus has a global ocean between its rocky core and icy crust, with signs of hydrothermal activity.
Hexagonal cloud patterns observed around Saturn's north pole.

timeline.text: Launch from Cape Canaveral carrying the Huygens probe.
First spacecraft to enter orbit around Saturn (UTC).
First close flyby of Enceladus and first hint of the plume.
Final (127th) close flyby of Titan; the Grand Finale begins.

chapters.text: I am Cassini, a big spacecraft about the size of a school bus. NASA, the European Space Agency and the Italian Space Agency made me together.
I was sent to study Saturn, its rings and its moons. I also carried a European probe called Huygens, which went down to the big moon Titan.
I circled Saturn for 13 years. I flew close to its moons many times to photograph and measure them.
I discovered fountains of water vapor and ice shooting out of the little moon Enceladus. Scientists think there is an ocean of water under its ice.
When my fuel was running low, I dove into Saturn's air on purpose in 2017 and burned up. That way I could never crash into a moon that might support life.

chapters.text: I am Cassini, the orbiter of the Cassini–Huygens mission, a cooperative project of NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Italian Space Agency (ASI). The Jet Propulsion Laboratory designed and assembled me. I launched on October 15, 1997, and entered orbit around Saturn on July 1, 2004.

My goals were to study Saturn, its magnetosphere and rings, Titan and the other icy moons. I carried ESA's Huygens probe, which landed on Titan on January 14, 2005 — the first landing in the outer Solar System.

During my first close flyby of Enceladus on February 17, 2005, a hint of something unusual appeared. With later flybys we detected a plume of water vapor and ice grains leaving its south pole at about 400 meters per second; some falls back onto the moon, and some feeds Saturn's E ring.

The mission gathered evidence for a global water ocean between the rocky core and icy crust of Enceladus, and signs of hydrothermal activity. The plume is a direct observation; the global ocean and its habitability are conclusions built on several measurements together.

As my propellant ran low, the team chose a safe ending: 22 weekly dives between Saturn and its rings, called the 'Grand Finale', and then a plunge into the atmosphere on September 15, 2017. I sent data until the end and burned up, protecting Enceladus and Titan from contamination.

glossary.meaning: The region around a planet controlled by its magnetic field.
One of Saturn's wide outer rings, supplied by material from the Enceladus plume.

rows: Escapes and forms Saturn's E ring

task.q: Some material falls back and some escapes. What does that suggest about the grains' speeds?
options: Grains have a range of speeds: some exceed the moon's escape speed and some don't
All grains move at exactly the same speed
task.explanation: 'About 400 m/s' is a rough average. A spread of speeds explains why some material returns while some feeds the ring.

questions.q: Which agency provided the Huygens probe?
questions.explanation: Huygens was a European probe, Cassini a NASA spacecraft, and ASI a mission partner. Giving accurate credit is part of scientific honesty.

questions.q: Why was the mission ended by diving into Saturn instead of leaving the spacecraft in orbit?
options: An uncontrolled spacecraft might one day hit a moon that could support life
Saturn would swallow it tomorrow anyway
To bring it back to Earth
questions.explanation: This is the principle of planetary protection. The final plunge also returned unique data from inside the atmosphere.

options: There is a global ocean under Enceladus's crust
Material is ejected at about 400 m/s
questions.explanation: The speed and landing date are measurements and events. The global ocean is a conclusion drawn from several lines of evidence.
